blocks.alt: Manifestos, Fear, and ‘Loser Thinking’: Inside Proton’s AI Reckoning

blocks.text: Proton 首席执行官 Andy Yen 在公司安全 Slack 频道里对一名员工发了话。这名员工当时建议，公司至少应该花几天时间对刚写好的代码做渗透测试，再上线。“这是扯淡，是失败者的思维。又快又安全当然可以做到，”Yen 在八月底的频道里写道。“别总想着怎么慢下来，多想想怎么快起来。”

inlines.text: Proton 首席执行官 Andy Yen 在公司安全 Slack 频道里对一名员工发了话。这名员工当时建议，公司至少应该花几天时间对刚写好的代码做渗透测试，再上线。“这是扯淡，是失败者的思维。又快又安全当然可以做到，”Yen 在八月底的频道里写道。“别总想着怎么慢下来，多想想怎么快起来。”

blocks.text: 在随后的一条消息里，Yen 重申了自己的观点：“只有失败者才会那么想。”他给团队的最终指示是“别再 lovingly handcrafting 我们所有的代码了，多用 AI。”

inlines.text: 在随后的一条消息里，Yen 重申了自己的观点：“只有失败者才会那么想。”他给团队的最终指示是“别再 lovingly handcrafting 我们所有的代码了，多用 AI。”

blocks.text: 这段对话只是众多例子之一，从中可以看出 Yen 和其他公司高管正如何大力推动 Proton 转向 AI。Proton 是一家瑞士公司，以加密邮件服务 Proton Mail 闻名，旗下还有一系列主打隐私与安全的产品，包括加密云盘、验证器应用、密码管理器等。

blocks.text: 过去几个月里，Yen 设立了一个邮箱地址，供员工在遇到任何阻碍 Proton 采用 AI 的事情时联系，以便管理层“无情地铲除一切阻挡 AI 速度的障碍”；Proton 在员工电脑上安装了软件，用来追踪公司生成了多少 AI 代码；Yen 还表示，今年是 Proton 最后一年招聘工程师，之后只招用 AI 来构建产品的人。

blocks.text: 这股 AI 推进势头在本周达到顶点：404 Media 报道称，Proton 表示将就员工使用 AI 的情况重新进行面谈，言下之意很明显——这些面谈以及员工是否愿意拥抱 AI，可能决定一个人会不会被解雇。

404 Media 报道
称，Proton 表示将就员工使用 AI 的情况重新进行面谈，言下之意很明显——这些面谈以及员工是否愿意拥抱 AI，可能决定一个人会不会被解雇。

blocks.text: 404 Media 采访了八名在职和一名已离职的 Proton 员工，并查阅了 Slack 聊天记录、会议录音以及公司 CTO 撰写的一份 AI 宣言。我们的报道揭示出 Proton 内部弥漫着恐惧文化：许多员工连对 Yen 的观点稍作批评、或讨论工程问题都犹豫不决。员工们描述的环境是：他们对安全问题、或被要求用 AI 开发安全产品确有真实担忧，却觉得自己无法发声，唯恐 Yen 当众斥责他们，或威胁他们的饭碗。

blocks.text: 他们表示：“很明显，Proton内部有些人对我们的方向不满，或者误解了它，还有很多人感到焦虑。我们决心快速推进，有时在向员工解释自己时过于生硬或过于迟缓。我们会改进这一点，因为他们的疑问正是我们最需要回答的。”

blocks.text: Yen曾是欧洲核子研究组织（CERN）的粒子物理学家，在公众面前展现出审慎的行事风格，但在内部，一名员工形容他更像一个“任性的孩子”。今年5月，Proton宣布将部署后量子密码学，以抵御未来量子计算机的攻击。这项工作耗费了数年努力，但有一个前提：至少目前，它不适用于旧邮件，只对功能上线后撰写的邮件生效。Proton把这一限制公之于众，让Yen很不高兴。

blocks.text: 他写道：“现在我们只剩下两个烂选择。要么把更重要的业务任务往后放，去重新加密旧邮件；要么因为不做这件事而不断在网上挨骂。所以也许你可以启发我一下，我们到底选哪个烂选择。”他补充说：“未来有两个选项。要么你们有足够的信心不把这搞砸，要么听我的建议确保它不被搞砸。”随后，他让团队的一名成员“去Reddit上”。

blocks.text: 自2014年斯诺登事件后推出Proton Mail以来，Proton不断推出新产品，使其更像一套办公套件，而不只是简单的电子邮件服务商。最近，这些产品聚焦于AI，推出了Lumo——一款大语言模型（LLM）聊天机器人，公司称它不会记录对话，也不会用用户数据训练模型。今年6月，Proton推出了其聊天机器人的2.0版本。

blocks.text: 在此之前，Yen 在公开场合对 AI 的表态还算温和。在八月接受《连线》采访时，他说 Proton 正在“打造 AI 功能和 AI 工具，因为我认为，如果隐私公司不设法介入、做出隐私优先的 AI，我们实际上就是把未来拱手让给那些并不真正为用户利益着想的科技公司”，并称公司正在“利用”外界对谷歌等企业化、侵犯隐私的 AI 的反弹情绪。去年，Yen 和 Proton 曾因他的一些言论受到批评，他当时暗示共和党和唐纳德·特朗普会比民主党更严厉地对待大型科技公司。

inlines.text: 根据 Slack 聊天记录和多名员工的讲述，到了八月底，Yen 在内部对 AI 的口风变了：Proton 要尽可能多地用 AI，而且要尽可能快。

blocks.text: “火车就要来了，要么上车，要么被碾过去。别当互联网时代的专业传真机操作员。”他在安全部门的 Slack 频道里写道，“我认为到今年年底，大多数开发者会停止写代码，转而开始为测试写规格说明，由 AI 来编写并运行这些测试，去验证 AI 写的代码——而人类已经无法再审查这些代码了。今年将是我们最后一年招聘工程师，从明年开始，我们要招的是过去称之为产品经理的人，用 AI 来造东西。”

blocks.text: AI 正在改变网络安全的运作方式：AI 智能体入侵公司系统，AI 协助发现重要代码中的巨大漏洞。隐私与安全领域的许多公司都在纠结如何应对 AI——无论是产品开发中怎么用，还是如何防御使用 AI 的黑客。有些公司可能会谨慎行事，另一些则为了利润而尽可能求快。这篇关于 Proton 自身如何面对 AI 的报道，为了解一家尤其受用户信任的安全公司内部正在发生什么，提供了前所未有的视角。

blocks.text: 起初，Proton 内部禁止使用 AI，但公司后来已批准 AI 用于内部各种场景，包括处理财务数据、在 Reddit 和 LinkedIn 上起草面向客户的回复，以及编写代码——“除非该源代码包含会给竞争对手带来直接优势的信息”，或涉及“创新或研发”，这是 404 Media 看到的一份 Proton 内部文件中的说法。根据 404 Media 获得的录音，Proton 首席技术官 Bart Butler 在一次会议上说，十月公司 90% 的代码由 AI 编写。多名员工告诉 404 Media，其中大部分代码是用 Anthropic 的 Claude 写的。Yen 也在 Slack 聊天中让员工使用 Claude。

blocks.text: Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, had a message for an employee in the company’s security Slack channel who urged the company to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. blocks.text: That exchange was just one of many that showed how Yen and other company executives are aggressively pushing Proton towards AI. blocks.text: 404 Media spoke to eight current and one former Proton employees and reviewed Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO. Our reporting reveals a culture of fear inside Proton, where many employees are hesitant to even mildly critique Yen’s views or discuss engineering problems. Workers describe an environment where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security products with AI, but feel unable to voice them, lest Yen berates them in front of everyone or threatens their employment at the company.

blocks.text: Yen, a former CERN particle physicist, projects a measured approach in public, but internally he acts more like what one employee described as a “petulant child.” In May, Proton announced it was implementing post-quantum cryptography which should protect against future attacks from quantum computers. The work took years of effort, with one caveat that it would not work on older emails, only those written after the feature’s launch, at least for the moment. Yen was not happy that Proton was drawing attention to this limitation.

blocks.text: Ever since launching Proton Mail in 2014 after the Snowden revelations, Proton has steadily introduced new products that make Proton more of a worksuite than a simple email provider. More recently, those products were focused around AI, with the launch of Lumo, a large language model (LLM) chatbot that the company says doesn’t log conversations or train on user data. In June, Proton launched a 2.0 version of its chatbot.

blocks.text: Up until this point, Yen’s public comments on AI were relatively tame. In an August interview with WIRED, he said Proton is “building AI features and AI tools, because I think if the privacy companies do not find a way to step in to build privacy-first AI, we are essentially ceding the future to tech companies that don’t have the best interests of users at heart,” and that the company was “capitalizing” on the backlash to corporatized, invasive AI from companies like Google. Last year, Yen and Proton were criticized for statements he made suggesting the Republican Party and Donald Trump would be harder on Big Tech than Democrats.

blocks.text: AI is changing how cybersecurity works, with AI agents hacking into companies, and AI assisting in the discovery of gaping vulnerabilities in important code. Many companies across the privacy and security space are grappling with how to deal with AI, either in the development of their products or how to defend themselves against hackers who are using AI. Some may do this carefully. Others are trying to do it as quickly as possible for profit. This account of Proton’s own reckoning with AI provides an unprecedented insight into what is happening inside one security-focused company users especially trust.

blocks.text: Initially, using AI was banned inside Proton, but the company has since approved AI for all sorts of use cases internally, including processing financial data, drafting customer-facing responses on Reddit and LinkedIn, and writing code “except when that source code contains information that would give immediate advantage to a competitor” or is related to “innovation or R&D [research and development],” according to an internal Proton document seen by 404 Media. Ninety percent of code at Proton in October was written by AI, the company’s CTO Bart Butler said in a meeting, according to audio 404 Media obtained. Much of that code is written with Anthropic’s Claude, multiple employees told 404 Media. And Yen tells employees in Slack chats to use Claude, too.

blocks.text: Earlier this week, Proton sent the email to employees saying they would re-interview workers about how they use AI in their jobs. The tone was clear; you may lose your job because of these interviews, current employees told 404 Media. “These re-interviews are consequential,” the email read. Soon after, a senior employee spoke up in Slack to Yen about the re-interviewing process. He suggested instead that Proton detect who is falling behind and support them and enforce high quality training.

blocks.text: Yen’s response was blunt: “Let’s put it this way, we already know more or less who is behind. If we were giving up on them, we would not bother with this process.”

blocks.text: The employee replied, “That messaging is fear-based. Which is probably why I suspect there are dozens of other employees watching us talk about this live and except for [other employee] no one else is chiming in.”

blocks.text: “People shouldn’t be scared to talk about this in public and to push back on you and leadership. A fear based culture feels like a cancer to me. It’s the opposite of engineering, you need to talk about things, even uncomfortable things,” they added. Yen eventually told the employee, in front of everyone: “If you are making the accusation that this is a financially driven decision and you don’t trust me when I tell you it’s not, then I think this might not be the place for you.”

blocks.text: The exchange with Yen was unusual not only in that someone was debating some of Yen’s ideas, but also that it directly referenced the culture of fear at Proton. “Whenever someone talks back to Andy it tends to be highlighted since very few people talk back to him,” one employee told 404 Media.
